prompt: `b := Book{Title: "Dom Casmurro"}`. What is in `b.Pages`, which the literal does not name?
hint: Lesson 6 printed a struct nobody filled in.

choices.text: Nothing: reading it panics until it is set
choices.why: Every field of a struct always holds a value; there is no unset state to panic about.

choices.text: `0`, the zero value of `int`
choices.why: Right. Fields a literal leaves out get their type's zero value; `%+v` printed `Pages:0`.

choices.text: The code does not compile: a literal must name every field
choices.why: A literal with field names may name any subset of them; only an unkeyed literal must give every value.

choices.text: Whatever value a constructor for `Book` sets
choices.why: Go runs no constructor when a struct is made. Zero is all there is unless your code sets more.

prompt: `type Book struct { Title string; Tags []string }`. What does `a == b` do for two `Book` values?
hint: A struct is comparable only if every field is.

choices.text: Compares `Title` and skips the slice
choices.why: Go never compares part of a struct; either every field is compared or the operator is refused.

choices.text: Compares both fields, the slice element by element
choices.why: Slices have no `==` at all, so a struct holding one cannot use the struct's `==` either.

choices.text: It does not compile, because of the slice field
choices.why: Right: `struct containing []string cannot be compared`. One slice field is enough to lose `==`.

choices.text: It compiles and panics when the program runs
choices.why: The type is known at compile time, so the refusal comes from the compiler, not at run time.

prompt: To print each field's name in front of its value, `fmt.Printf` takes the verb `___`.
hint: `%v` with one more character.

prompt: `go vet` reported `net.TCPAddr{ip, 8080, ""}` and would not report `Point{3, 4}` for your own `Point`. Why the difference?
hint: Who can change each type, and who would have to fix the literal?

choices.text: A field added to another package's type breaks your literal; your own type changes with your code
choices.why: Right. The check covers struct types imported from another package, whose authors decide when fields are added.

choices.text: Unkeyed literals are always wrong, and vet only has time for the standard library
choices.why: Any imported package counts, not only the standard library, and your own small types are a reasonable place for them.

choices.text: An unkeyed literal of `TCPAddr` compiles to a different value
choices.why: It produced `127.0.0.1:8080` as intended; the warning is about the future, not today's value.

choices.text: `Point` has only two fields
choices.why: The number of fields is not what vet counts; it asks where the type was declared.

prompt: Which of these types can be the key of a map? Choose all that apply.
hint: Lesson 14's rule, applied field by field.

choices.text: `struct{ X, Y int }`
choices.why: Yes. Both fields are comparable, so the struct is; `map[Point]int` counted visits.

choices.text: `struct{ Title string; Tags []string }`
choices.why: No. The slice field makes the whole struct incomparable.

choices.text: `[2]struct{ X, Y int }`
choices.why: Yes. An array of comparable elements is comparable, and these elements are.

choices.text: `struct{ Name string; Seen map[string]bool }`
choices.why: No. A map field can only be compared to `nil`, so the struct cannot be compared at all.

prompt: A `User` has a field `age int`, lower case. What does `json.Marshal` do with it?
hint: The output had no `age` in it. What did `err` say?

choices.text: Writes it under the key `age`
choices.why: The output had no `age` key at all.

choices.text: Returns an error naming the field
choices.why: `err` printed `<nil>`. Nothing reports the missing field.

choices.text: Leaves it out, and reports nothing
choices.why: Right. Another package cannot see a lower-case name, so the field is skipped in silence.

choices.text: Writes it as `null`, since its value cannot be read
choices.why: `null` was what the nil slice `Tags` gave. `age` did not appear in any form.

prompt: What does the tag `json:"-"` on a `Password` field do?
hint: Compare the plain `User` with the tagged one.

choices.text: Writes the field under the key `-`
choices.why: A tag of exactly `-` means the opposite: the field is not written. The documentation gives a different spelling for a key named `-`.

choices.text: Leaves the field out only when it is empty
choices.why: That is `omitempty`. With `-`, `hunter2` was not written either.

choices.text: Writes the field with its value masked
choices.why: `encoding/json` has no masking; the key is simply absent.

choices.text: Keeps it out of the JSON always
choices.why: Right. The password set to `hunter2` did not appear in either output.

prompt: Match each tag to what `json.Marshal` does with the field.
hint: The first word is a name; what follows the comma is an option.

pairs.right: Written as `email`, or left out when empty
Written as `ended`, or left out when it holds its type's zero value

prompt: A field `Name string` has the tag `json: "name"`, with a space after the colon. What happens?
hint: Which tool read the tags in the section?

choices.text: The compiler refuses the tag
choices.why: To the compiler a tag is a string like any other; `go run` built and ran it.

choices.text: Key `Name`, and `go vet` flags the tag
choices.why: Right. The tag is unreadable, so the default name is used, and vet says `bad syntax for struct tag value`.

choices.text: The key comes out as `name`; the space is ignored
choices.why: The output was `{"Name":"Ana",…}`: the space made the whole tag unreadable.

choices.text: `json.Marshal` returns an error about the tag
choices.why: It returned the JSON with no complaint; only `go vet` complained.

prompt: A field `Deadline time.Time` tagged `json:"deadline,omitempty"` is left at its zero value. What does `json.Marshal` write?
hint: Is a struct ever "empty" in `omitempty`'s sense?

choices.text: Nothing, because the zero time is empty
choices.why: `omitempty` knows false, 0, nil and length zero. A struct is none of those, so it is written.

choices.text: `"deadline": null`
choices.why: A `time.Time` is a struct value, never nil, so it cannot come out as `null`.
Right. That is what happened to `started`; `ended`, tagged `omitzero` instead, was left out.

choices.text: An empty string, `"deadline":""`
choices.why: The zero time is written as a real instant, the first of year 1, not as an empty string.

prompt: A struct has `ID int` tagged `json:"id"` = 0, `Note string` tagged `json:"note,omitempty"` = "", `token string` = "abc", `Tags []string` tagged `json:"tags,omitempty"` = `[]string{"x"}` and `Score int` tagged `json:"score"` = 0. How many keys does `json.Marshal` write?
hint: Without `omitempty`, a zero is still written.

prompt: Put the three parts of a tagged struct field in the order they are written.
hint: The same order as a `var` declaration, plus one.

prompt: `json.Unmarshal` reads `{"name": "Bia", "nickname": "b"}` into a `User` with no `nickname` field. What happens to `"nickname"`?
hint: What did `err` print?

choices.text: `Unmarshal` returns `json: unknown field "nickname"`
choices.why: That message only came from a `Decoder` told to `DisallowUnknownFields`. Plain `Unmarshal` returned nil.

choices.text: It is skipped, and the error is nil
choices.why: Right. Unknown keys are ignored by default.

choices.text: It is stored in the closest field, `Name`
choices.why: `Name` received `Bia`. Matching ignores case, nothing more.

choices.text: The program panics
choices.why: Nothing panicked; the run printed the struct and `<nil>`.

prompt: A field is tagged `json:"name"` and the JSON says `"NAME": "Bia"`. What does `encoding/json` put in the field?
hint: It prefers an exact match. What if there is none?

choices.text: Nothing: the key must match the tag exactly
choices.why: That is version 2's rule. `encoding/json` filled `Name` with `Bia`.

choices.text: `BIA`, upper-cased to match the key
choices.why: Only the key is compared without case; the value is copied as it is.

choices.text: `Bia`
choices.why: Right. With no exact match, a key differing only in case is accepted.

choices.text: An error about the case of the key
choices.why: `err` was nil. Case is not something `encoding/json` complains about.

prompt: After `dec := json.NewDecoder(r)`, calling `dec.___()` makes `Decode` refuse keys that match no field.
hint: It names the thing it disallows.

prompt: Somebody writes `json.Unmarshal(data, u)`, forgetting the `&`. What happens?
hint: Separate the compiler, the run and `go vet`.

choices.text: The compiler refuses a non-pointer argument
choices.why: `Unmarshal` accepts a value of any type, so the compiler has nothing to object to.

choices.text: It fills a copy of `u`, and `u` stays empty with a nil error
choices.why: The error was not nil: it said `json: Unmarshal(non-pointer main.User)`.

choices.text: An error at run time, which `go vet` predicts
choices.why: Right: `call of Unmarshal passes non-pointer as second argument`.

choices.text: It panics with a nil dereference
choices.why: There is no nil pointer involved; `Unmarshal` checks its argument and returns an error.

prompt: `User` has one field, `Name string` tagged `json:"name"`. Which inputs make `json.Unmarshal` return an error? Choose all that apply.
hint: Unknown and missing keys are not errors.

choices.why: Yes: `cannot unmarshal number into Go struct field User.name of type string`.

choices.text: `{"name": "Bia", "age": 30}`
choices.why: No. `age` matches no field and is skipped.
No. A missing key leaves the field at zero, which is not an error.

choices.text: `{"name": "Bia",}`
choices.why: Yes. A comma before the closing brace is not JSON: `invalid character '}'`.

prompt: A service reads its configuration with `json.Unmarshal` into a struct with `Timeout int` tagged `json:"timeout"`. An operator types `"timeuot": 30`. What happens, and what would have caught it?
hint: The key matches no field. What does the default do with such a key?

choices.text: `Unmarshal` returns an error naming `timeuot`, and the service refuses to start until somebody fixes the file
choices.why: Plain `Unmarshal` skips unknown keys and returns nil; only a strict `Decoder` names them.

choices.text: `Timeout` gets 30, since key matching is forgiving
choices.why: It forgives case, not spelling: `timeuot` and `timeout` are different words.

choices.text: `Timeout` stays 0, no error; `DisallowUnknownFields` would refuse it
choices.why: Right. A file a person typed is the case the section gave for refusing unknown keys.

choices.text: `go vet` reports the misspelt key
choices.why: vet reads the Go source, tags included; it never sees a JSON file read at run time.

prompt: The same `{"NAME": "Bia"}` goes through `jsonv2.Unmarshal` from `encoding/json/v2`, into a field tagged `json:"name"`. What comes back?
hint: Version 2 changed one rule about names.

choices.text: `Name` is `Bia`, as with `encoding/json`
choices.why: The run printed `{Name: Tags:[]}` for version 2: it matches names exactly.

choices.text: `Name` stays empty, and the error is nil
choices.why: Right. `NAME` is not `name` to version 2, and an unknown key is still not an error by default.

choices.text: An error about an unknown member
choices.why: Version 2 also ignores unknown keys unless told otherwise; both errors printed `<nil>`.

choices.text: It does not compile: both packages are named `json` in their package clause
choices.why: Importing the second one as `jsonv2` gives it another name, and the program ran.

prompt: `Tags []string` tagged `json:"tags"` is nil, and `encoding/json` writes `"tags":null`. The reader expects a list. What makes it write `[]`?
hint: Lesson 12 marshalled both kinds of empty slice.

choices.text: Adding `omitempty` to the tag
choices.why: `omitempty` removes the key altogether, which a reader expecting a list handles no better than `null`.

choices.text: Setting it to `[]string{}` before marshalling
choices.why: Right. An empty slice that is not nil is written as `[]`; only the nil one becomes `null`.

choices.text: Nothing: `encoding/json` writes every empty slice as `null`
choices.why: Lesson 12 printed `null []`: the nil slice and the empty one come out differently.

choices.text: Tagging it `json:"tags,omitzero"` instead of `json:"tags"`
choices.why: A nil slice is its type's zero value, so `omitzero` drops the key instead of writing `[]`.
